📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Richard Hughes made a lot of mistakes when he was Liverpool's sporting director.

The Englishman spent well over £600 million on new players and, it's still unclear whether their team is any better off.

So, even though Hughes did quite well with some of the deals he made, he obviously had to make a few mistakes on the way.

Right now, Liverpool's entire team could still do with upgrading but, because they have a handful of players who's contract are going to expire in June 2027, they've taken priority.

The January transfer window is now just over a month away so, some transfers are going to have to take place soon, otherwise, the Reds will be left even further behind their title rivals than they currently find themselves.

Julian Ward can sign Luka Vuskovic after Richard Hughes chose against it in the summer.

Liverpool's defence has been one of the main areas that Liverpool have tried to strengthen over the last few years.

Virgil van Dijk, Andy Robertson and Joe Gomez are just a few examples of the older players that they were using last season.

And, with Robertson gone and the other two having their contracts expire in June 2027, another defensive rebuild could be on the way.

Many different links with players have emerged recently with Giorgio Scalvini one of them.

However, a recent patch from Florian Plettenberg on Luka Vuskovic's situation is something that should definitely pique the interest of Liverpool and their fanbase.

"Liverpool have Luka Vuskovic on their shortlist for next summer. The 19 y/o top defender is being monitored regularly," he shared via X.

"His contract at Brighton is valid until 2031. No release clause will be available next summer. Current price valuation: around €100m (+/-).

According to recent reports, "Vuskovic is very happy under Fabian Hürzeler. However, his dream is to join Real Madrid one day.

Liverpool need to sign Luka Vuskovic.

Vuskovic has been a revelation since joining Brighton.

The Croatian had a spectacular season last term while on loan with Hamburger SV with most people thinking that Tottenham would welcome him back with open arms.

However, that didn't end up happening and, instead of keeping the 19-year-old around, Roberto de Zerbi chose to bring Jan Paul Van Hecke through the welcome doors instead.

And, while the Dutchman's performances have been impressive, Vuskovic has probably been the better player.

He's transformed Fabian Hurzeler's defence and, there's no wonder why the Seagulls want a record deal for the centre-back.

Obviously, it's a lot of money to spend on a defender who's only had one season of Premier League experience but, if they did manage to get a deal over the line, Ward would be instantly rectifying a problem that Hughes made for himself.

It would also be a sure-fire way for the Englishman to get fans on his side as, during the summer, most Liverpool fans wanted their club to sign him.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Two of the Premier League's most successful clubs renew their fierce rivalry on Sunday as Liverpool welcome Manchester United to Anfield for their first meeting of the season.
  • The Reds are navigating a period of transition under Andoni Iraola, but have made an encouraging start to the campaign, climbing to fourth in the Premier League table with 18 points.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Saikat Mandal | 21 Nov 2026 15:08.

Two of the Premier League's most successful clubs renew their fierce rivalry on Sunday as Liverpool welcome Manchester United to Anfield for their first meeting of the season.

The Reds are navigating a period of transition under Andoni Iraola, but have made an encouraging start to the campaign, climbing to fourth in the Premier League table with 18 points.

Manchester United, meanwhile, have endured their worst start to a upcoming season, prompting the club hierarchy to part ways with Michael Carrick, who guided them into the Champions League places last term.

The Red Devils have wasted little time in appointing Mauricio Pochettino as his successor, but the Argentine faces a daunting introduction to the rivalry, having won just three of his 19 managerial meetings with Liverpool.

Here, Sports Mole provides everything you need to know about how to tune into the contest.

Liverpool vs Man Utd is one of two Premier League fixtures scheduled for Sunday, with the other seeing Hull City welcome Brighton & Hove Albion.

The eagerly anticipated clash at Anfield is scheduled to get underway at 4.30pm UK time, a prime Sunday afternoon slot that should allow supporters both in the stands and watching from around the world to savour one of English football's biggest rivalries.

Liverpool vs Man Utd will take place at Anfield, the 61,276-capacity stadium that has served as the spiritual home of the mighty Reds since 1892.

Anfield is the fifth-largest football stadium in England and has been the setting for countless memorable encounters between these fierce rivals, with its famous atmosphere often adding another layer of intensity.

Beyond football, the iconic venue also opens its doors to major musical events during the off-season, with global superstar Taylor Swift among the big-name artists to have performed there during her record-breaking Eras Tour.

Non-Sky customers can stream the contest through a NOW Day or cancel-anytime Month pass, while viewers in India can catch the action live on JioHotstar.

Liverpool and Man Utd's official X accounts are expected to share match snippets throughout the contest, while journalists covering the game may also post their own footage and updates.

After the final whistle, extended highlights should be available on both clubs' official YouTube channels, while viewers in the UK can catch the action again on BBC's Match of the Day 2.

Liverpool have an opportunity to cut the gap to Manchester City to just one point with victory on Sunday, giving them an added incentive to make home advantage count.

The Reds have endured an uncomfortable run against their fiercest rivals at Anfield, having failed to beat the Red Devils on home soil since their emphatic 7-0 triumph in March 2023, and Iraola will be desperate to put that unwanted sequence behind them by claiming all three points.

The likes of Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz will be eager to rise to the occasion and deliver on a stage of such magnitude, but Liverpool's overriding priority is to turn their home performances into consistent results and strengthen their position in the title race.

For Man Utd, the stakes are arguably even higher, with the visitors desperate to climb out of the relegation zone and give their troubled campaign some much-needed impetus.

Pochettino, meanwhile, will be keen to mark the beginning of his Man Utd tenure with a statement victory, although he could hardly have been handed a more demanding opening assignment; given the circumstances, even a hard-earned draw at Anfield would represent a respectable start to his reign.

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the fresh coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

In a recent development, “Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”.

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso noted: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

In a recent development, “We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”.

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding upcoming ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

How different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

It cannot be overlooked how this win owed a debt to the erratic refereeing of Paul Tierney, especially the amnesty he offered to Morgan Rogers on the stroke of half-time.

The home team’s argument that this was a potential game changer was supported when the England midfielder was inevitably involved in the move which led to Neto breaking through 44 seconds into the second half – a lead Chelsea never looked like surrendering as Everton’s attacking limitations were exposed.

Industry observers note that he told the  press: “I wish him the best recovery. We won’t set timelines, but we expect him to be out for several weeks. It’s not going to be short. Whether it’s before or after Christmas then time will tell. It needs to be done properly.”.

Recent findings suggest that he is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is important and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”.

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

Recent findings suggest that in his press conference ahead of the weekend, Everton boss David Moyes was not too concerned by his relatively small squad.He remarked:  “Leicester City won the league with not too many players. We have not got too many players. I am not saying we’re going to win the league, but we want to try to challenge and be around the top teams.”.

Industry observers note that that might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

It has been revealed that chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Sources indicate that next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

In a recent development, david Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

Arsenal 1-0 Hull: Not efficient, but enough

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in yesterday’s preview blog, I spoke about Arsenal’s attacking efficiency, and how that might be key to taking all three points.
  • According to recent reports, despite generally dominating possession, I thought there was a lack of precision in certain aspects of our first half play.
  • Industry observers note that and then there was Kai Havertz.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in yesterday’s preview blog, I spoke about Arsenal’s attacking efficiency, and how that might be key to taking all three points. In yesterday’s game against Hull, Arsenal took 21 shots, 10 of which were on target, and scored one goal from that. Efficient?

According to recent reports, despite generally dominating possession, I thought there was a lack of precision in certain aspects of our first half play. Passes weren’t quite quick enough or accurate enough, but there were moments when we could have found the breakthrough. Gabriel almost got on the end of a Noni Madueke cross which was flicked on towards the back post, Rice had a tame shot from a free kick before a late header which he probably should have done better with.

Industry observers note that and then there was Kai Havertz. It’s fair to say Hull didn’t leave a lot of room behind a defensive line that often had six players stretched across it, but late in the half a superb Martin Odegaard pass sent him clean through, one on one with the keeper. I haven’t seen replays but in real time I felt like he should have pulled the trigger – instead he over-complicated it. You have to be prepared to shoot from there, even if it’s on your wrong foot.

In a recent development, then there was a penalty incident when he complained vociferously, play went on, the ref was then told to go to the screen and we all assumed it would be a penalty. However, the ref remarked it was a foul but Havertz was offside – and it felt like a massive waste of time. Afterwards, it emerged it should have been a penalty, but apparently the rule is ‘open to interpretation’. So clear as mud then.

In the second half, we seemed to play down our right a lot, with Madueke the outlet most of the time. I thought he did pretty well, much better than Christos Tzolis on the other side, but the breakthrough wouldn’t come. Mikel Merino replaced Rice (who seemed to be on the end of a wild challenge in midfield that the ref just ignored as he tumbled through the air), and Viktor Gyokeres came on for Havertz.

Recent findings suggest that on 71 minutes though, we found the goal. Madueke’s shot was spilled by the keeper, Odegaard was quickest to react to poke the ball home for 1-0. And to be fair, you always felt confident that would be enough. We are the masters of the single goal margin win, and this was another one. Not a day that will live long in the memory or anything, but a 1-0 win that takes us into the Interlull in really good shape, and there’s not much arguing with that.

Or really, much more to say about this game. Mikel Arteta sounded happy enough, saying:.

I’m delighted with the win. To go into the international break with a win is one of the best things about being a coach or player, I would say. Regarding the performance, I thought we were the better team, had enough chances to score and make it bigger for ourselves and we weren’t efficient enough to take them.

We then had to rely on generating volume, plenty of persisting until we finally broke them down. Martin then got the goal. Not the most beautiful one, but the most effective one, a simple ‘shoot and then follow the next action’, and that was ultimately enough to win the game.

So Arsenal sit top of the table, with 9 wins from 10 so far this season in the league, and it’s a very impressive run of form. Do I wish we had more attacking potency? Absolutely, and I do worry a bit that it might bite us in the arse somewhere down the line, but for now, we can see that this is a team that just knows how to win, and perhaps that’s the most important thing.

Recent findings suggest that right, I’m gonna leave it there for this morning. I have to head back to Dublin today. It was great to see lots of you over the weekend, until next time! And we’ll have an Arsecast Extra for you tomorrow too.

Opinion: Liverpool ready to sign their next Jeremy Jacquet, he's perfect

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The young Frenchman was brought in for around £55 million with plenty of fans, pundits and journalists all saying that Liverpool had spent too much on a player who'd never played outside of France.
  • The fact that he was only 20 years old didn't help matters much either.
  • However, to the surprise of many, he took becoming a Liverpool player in his stride and has arguably been one of their best performers this term.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jeremy Jacquet has been a revelation at Liverpool.

The young Frenchman was brought in for around £55 million with plenty of fans, pundits and journalists all saying that Liverpool had spent too much on a player who'd never played outside of France.

The fact that he was only 20 years old didn't help matters much either.

However, to the surprise of many, he took becoming a Liverpool player in his stride and has arguably been one of their best performers this term.

He's far better than Ibrahima Konate ever was and, he's still got another decade left as a top-level player.

So, the fact that Liverpool are ready to sign their next version of him is rather exciting.

Liverpool have entered the transfer race for Giorgio Scalvini.

Liverpool's defence may have had a decent chunk of change spent on it over the last couple of years but, there are still a couple of problem areas that they need to fix.

For example, both Kostas Tsimikas and Milos Kerkez have massively underperformed this season.

Every time one of them is played, fans want the other to come back in and take their place.

Obviously, this isn't ideal considering Kerkez was expected to be the Reds' next Andy Robertson.

However, the centre of their defence also has a couple of question marks hanging over it thanks to the undecided futures of Virgil van Dijk and Joe Gomez.

So, Liverpool being linked with Giorgio Scalvini is hardly a surprised, especially with how much potential he has to fulfil.

"Manchester United, Liverpool and Chelsea are positioning themselves to make a possible move for Atalanta defensive star Giorgio Scalvini, with the highly-rated Italian emerging as a major potential transfer target for 2027, TEAMtalk can exclusively reveal," TEAMtalk wrote.

"TEAMtalk understands that a number of English sides are now carrying out detailed work on Scalvini as the possibility of him finally leaving Atalanta gathers momentum.

"Newcastle United are long-term admirers of the Italy international, but the latest interest is coming from Manchester United, Liverpool and Chelsea, who have all been monitoring his development.

"United and Liverpool are both assessing their central defensive options as they consider potential reinforcements, with Scalvini increasingly emerging as a player of interest to their recruitment departments.".

Giorgio Scalvini could become Liverpool's next Jeremy Jacquet.

Scalvini has been linked with an exit from Atalanta for a fair few years now.

Ever since he broke into their first team back in the 2021/22 season, the Italian has been of interest to many different clubs around the globe.

However, now that Liverpool have proven that they're giving youngsters a go in their starting XI with their use of Jacquet and others such as Trey Nyoni, they have more ground to stand on than other clubs.

Of course, Scalvini is a tad older than Jacquet at 22 years old but, since they're both young and have a lot of their careers left to go, it's clear to see why the Italian could become Liverpool's next Jacquet.

He also plays as the right-sided centre-back in a back four so, he'd fit straight into Andoni Iraola's aims if they chose to bring him in.

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I watched Man Utd v Aston Villa last night.
  • This is someone who has managed over 1000 games in his career.
  • Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, it looks as if Pierre Sage is gonna get fired by Crystal Palace and replaced by Thomas Frank.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I watched Man Utd v Aston Villa last night. When Villa conceded late on to let a two goal lead slip for the second time in the game, Unai Emery threw a strop and went down the tunnel. It’s not the first time he’s eschewed a handshake with the opposition manager, and his post-game interview where he insisted he thought the game was over was very funny because it was such obvious bullshit.

This is someone who has managed over 1000 games in his career. I’m pretty sure he knows when the final whistle blows and when it doesn’t. Can you imagine if Mikel Arteta did that? You wouldn’t be able to move for all the opinion pieces about what a sore loser he is and all the rest. But perhaps Emery gets a pass because he is ‘the best manager in the league’. Anyway, perhaps it provides a stay of execution for Michael Carrick at Man Utd, which can only be a good thing.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, it looks as if Pierre Sage is gonna get fired by Crystal Palace and replaced by Thomas Frank. That seems a sensible appointment to me. Enough time has passed since his spell at Sp*rs for the toxins to wear off, and he’s clearly a good manager. I’ve never been convinced by Sage, I just think he looks too scruffy. As if someone got a 10 year old to draw man and brought it to life.

I quite enjoyed this quote from Mikel Arteta in his post-game press conference after Saturday’s 1-0 win over Hull:.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes we try to score the perfect goal against low blocks, but we need to be much more chaotic than that. If we open the scoring much earlier also, it changes the game.

I love it as a concept, adding some chaos to our control makes a lot of sense, but it also kinda seems at odds with what the manager asks of his players. Maybe he just means more shots from distance, maybe riskier pass when we’re trying to break the opposition down, or maybe there’s something he’s got cooking for over the Interlull and when we return we see something we never expected. He did kick the shit out of a dugout chair on Saturday, that’s a upcoming enough development to be fair.

I wonder was he referring to the Kai Havertz chance in the first half, when he could have shot on his right foot but tried to cut back/lay it off. If you shoot, maybe you don’t score but as we saw with the winning goal from Martin Odegaard, it might end up in the path of another Arsenal player who can finish it off. Perhaps too there’s a bit of a through line between being more chaotic and what Noni Madueke is doing at the moment. He can be a bit scattergun, but as Nick Wright points out on Sky Sports, his numbers are improving. I don’t think Arteta will ever embrace full chaos, all the time, but if he can add a little more to the mix, it could certainly help.

Right, I have to leave it there for this morning. A bit shorter than normal, I know. We will have an Arsecast Extra for you a bit later on though. We’ve already put out the call for questions on BlueSky @gunnerblog.bsky.social and @arseblog.com, so fire away using the hashtag #arsecastextra – or if you’re an Arseblog Member on Patreon, leave your question in the #arsecast-extra-questions channel on our Discord server.

The pod should be out around around lunchtime. Until then, have a good one.

Chelsea suffer new Moises Caicedo injury blow as Xabi Alonso forced into early Leeds change

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Ben Knapton | 21 Nov 2026 15:24, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 15:43.
  • Chelsea have been dealt yet another injury blow concerning Moises Caicedo, who was forced off in the first half of Saturday's Premier League clash with Leeds United.
  • The 25-year-old was making his sixth start of the top-flight season at Stamford Bridge, joining Romeo Lavia in the centre of the park, but his race was run with just 22 minutes gone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 21 Nov 2026 15:24, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 15:43.

Chelsea have been dealt yet another injury blow concerning Moises Caicedo, who was forced off in the first half of Saturday's Premier League clash with Leeds United.

The 25-year-old was making his sixth start of the top-flight season at Stamford Bridge, joining Romeo Lavia in the centre of the park, but his race was run with just 22 minutes gone.

Caicedo was involved in a heavy mid-air collision with James Justin early doors and was left in a heap on the ground, but he was ultimately able to carry on, albeit briefly.

The Ecuador international sat down on the turf just moments later and covered his face with his arm as he was attended to by medical staff, before hobbling off the field to be replaced by Jordan Henderson.

Caicedo appeared to be struggling with a back injury and was given an ice pack as he sat down on the bench, shortly before the Blues took the lead through Emmanuel Emegha.

The severity of Caicedo's latest concern is yet to be ascertained, and it may well be that the South American simply sustained a contact injury which will heal in a matter of days.

However, the midfielder's withdrawal prolonged a painful stop-start season, in which he has already missed six games across the Premier League and EFL Cup due to two separate injuries.

Sources indicate that caicedo sat out Chelsea's opening two games vs. Fulham and Luton Town owing to a knock, before picking up a calf problem just 14 minutes into his first appearance of the campaign against Brighton & Hove Albion.

The Blues faced Leeds (in the EFL Cup), Arsenal, Hull City and Brentford without Caicedo due to his new calf problem, since when he has been a mainstay in Alonso's midfield with the captain's armband.

The Ecuadorian is now an early doubt for next Friday's trip to Nottingham Forest, though, as well as Chelsea's London derby at home to Crystal Palace on December 2.

Caicedo's fitness struggles in the 2026-27 season are uncharacteristic, as the 25-year-old missed just two games through injury or illness in his first three campaigns at the club.

Both of those absences occurred in his debut 2023-24 campaign, in which he missed a 0-0 draw with Bournemouth because of a knock, and a 2-1 defeat to Wolverhampton Wanderers due to illness.

Caicedo navigated the entire 2024-25 season without picking up an injury, starting all 38 Premier League games and being omitted from several Conference League squads to enjoy a well-earned rest.

The midfielder then made another 50 appearances in the 2025-26 season, and his only notable absences were due to suspension rather than fitness problems.

Alonso is already missing Joao Pedro, Jamie Gittens, Maxence Lacroix, Jorrel Hato and Reece James, and none is expected to return before the end of the month.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we’re two days into the final Interlull of the year and, as you might expect, there’s not a huge amount going on. The senior fixtures don’t start until Thursday, so we haven’t even got a fresh batch of international press conference quotes to sink our teeth into. Slim pickings.

In a recent development, this time around, 20 of our 25 first-team players have been selected, which is a pretty remarkable tally. All the more so when you consider Noni Madueke can count himself unlucky to have missed out for England, while Bukayo Saka and William Saliba would ordinarily be shoo-ins.

According to recent reports, any concerns about the Frenchman’s absence against Hull, having travelled to Prague in midweek, were eased the following morning when he lined up for the under-21s against Aston Villa in Premier League 2. More minutes in his legs, rather than another injury to worry about.

Bolstered by Saliba and Max Dowman, whose domestic suspension kept him out of Saturday’s game, the youngsters ran out 5-2 winners. Given they’re currently 21st out of 31 teams in their Swiss-style league table, perhaps this is the way forward. Send the major guns down a level and start battering our way towards more club silverware. Relentless madman Arteta, finding upcoming frontiers for his evil genius. He doesn’t just leave his technical area. He thinks outside it.

In a recent development, if you missed it, Max has been promoted to England’s under-21s for this window. He’ll join Arsenal loanees Tommy Setford and Ethan Nwaneri, as well as former Hale Enders Brooke Norton-Cuffy, who came off the bench for Hull on Saturday, and Amario Cozier-Duberry, who seems to be doing well at Middlesbrough on loan from Brighton.

Given Max has been in and around Mikel Arteta’s first team for a couple of seasons now, it’s easy to take milestones like this for granted. But playing under-21 international football at 16 is another significant step, even for someone whose talent has made rapid progress seem almost routine.

Sources indicate that back in September, Lee Carsley described his eventual promotion as inevitable, while stressing that the timing had to be right. The point was to bring him into a squad where he could play and compete, rather than move him up simply because everyone expected it.

Carsley referenced Nwaneri when discussing the temptation to push exceptional youngsters through the age groups. His point was that the aim is a long senior career, not winning a race to the first cap. That seems sensible enough. Max doesn’t need every appearance to become an audition for the next level.

A couple of games against Portugal and France should be a useful challenge in their own right. Carsley and Arteta also know each other from their Everton days, which ought to help when discussing what he needs.

Industry observers note that with England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland hosting Euro 2028, you can imagine that tournament already features somewhere in Max’s ambitions. There’s plenty of football between now and then, though. For the moment, let’s see how he gets on with this next step.

It has been revealed that elsewhere, most of our European internationals will be occupied with the Nations League, while the South American trio rack up the air miles again. Piero Hincapie heads home to Ecuador for friendlies against Costa Rica and Bolivia, while Gabriel and Bruno Guimaraes face Japan and Singapore, both in Singapore.

Recent findings suggest that I appreciate Brazil’s options are more limited when European teams are tied up with UEFA fixtures, but their friendly schedule does sometimes feel like somebody has thrown a dart at a map. No doubt the commercial logic is compelling, but that doesn’t make you any less worried about tired hamstrings.

Anyway, fingers crossed they all come back with their limbs intact.

In other news, Italian publication Tuttosport has named Andrea Berta the winner of its Best Executive Award at this year’s Golden Boy Awards. The Arsenal sporting director collects the gong three transfer windows into his tenure, the latest of which ended with some fans calling for his head after the failed pursuits of Vinicius Junior and Julian Alvarez.

Industry observers note that either the bar is pretty low, he’s basking in the reflected glory of the team’s success, or it’s one of those shindigs where buying an inordinately expensive table guarantees you something shiny to take home. The cynic in me wasn’t exactly silenced by the news that Joan Laporta won Best President and Jorge Mendes Best Agent. In fact, I snorted when I read that. And lest we forget, Edu picked up a similar award from the same organisers in 2023….

It has been revealed that myles Lewis-Skelly was in contention for the actual Golden Boy award, which went to Barcelona defender Pau Cubarsi. Hard to argue too much with that, given the 19-year-old was at the heart of Spain’s World Cup win.

Cubarsi also made the FIFPRO World 11. More pertinently for us, so did David Raya. Having finished second to compatriot Unai Simon in the Ballon d’Or’s Best Goalkeeper category, I imagine there’s some satisfaction in getting the nod from the people who actually play the game. More than 26,000 professionals from 75 countries cast their votes, which is a fairly substantial dressing room to win over.

Alessia Russo, who is in fine form even if Arsenal Women are not, also earned her third selection for the Women’s World 11.

In a recent development, as you’ll have gathered from the snippiness above, I find it easy to be cynical about these things. There are so many awards now that you half expect to get one for finding your seat at the ceremony. Still, sometimes it’s nice to give people a pat on the back and recognise a job well done.

On an entirely unrelated note, have you voted for us to win Best Fan Media at the upcoming FSA Awards? You’ve only got a week left. A prestigious honour, that one. 😉.

Right, I think that’s as much toothpaste as I can squeeze out of a slow news day. If anything else happens, we’ll have it covered on Arseblog News. Catch you next time.

Published: 11:37 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 11:44 EST, 20 November 2026.

Derek McInnes can be understood in wanting a quiet January window. He’s still bonding a squad of players together. Drama and diversions are the last thing he needs when there looks to be an opportunity to win a title on the horizon.

In the case of Olwethu Makhanya, for example, this is definitely not the time to sell.

The 22-year-old South African has been impressive at centre-back, but it will take a campaign catching the attention in high-level European football for him to raise his value to Calvin Bassey levels and beyond.

Same goes for the likes of Ryan Naderi. Getting into the Czechia squad and increasing his range of experience makes him a more interesting prospect, but UEFA competition is a platform that ought to increase his premium.

McInnes, as he did this week, has to say he wants to keep his more prominent talents anyway. It would be strange to appear accepting of the board cashing in on bigger players.

In a recent development, when it comes to Nico Raskin, however, things are different. A buyer for him should have been found in the summer after his World Cup involvement with Belgium.

Rangers midfielder Nico Raskin is an asset who could be sold in the January transfer window.

From the chit-chat around the game, it does not seem unreasonable to think Rangers maybe overvalued him in the initial part of that window and missed the boat in terms of securing a sale.

It has been revealed that if he stays for the rest of this season and enters the final year of his contract, though, the money you can ask for naturally reduces. The club might seek to tie him up on a new deal, of course, but his remarks about being ‘mentally ready to leave’ at the start of the season point to the most likely direction of travel.

Industry observers note that is he irreplaceable? Not at all. And this is where forward planning should come into the mix.

If there’s someone out there willing to edge anywhere close to the £15m mark for the 25-year-old, they should be getting sounded out now – with a contingency proposal being discussed and worked on in tandem.

Yes, Rangers need to get back to winning silverware, but the need to start raising funds through selling players – and replacing them - at appropriate times is pressing too.

As often mentioned here, they can’t keep spending money the way they have been without considerably more coming back in return.

Sources indicate that raskin’s a good player, but his three-and-a-half years at Ibrox have hardly been shaped by his propensity for winning medals, have they? If a realistic fee is there in January, there’s a case to make for it being taken.

Breaking: Zubimendi addresses tiredness and transfer talk

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1313 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Martin’s Day in Germany, a day I’d never heard of until I had a child over here.
  • Martin was, as the story goes, a 4th-Century Roman soldier and is best known for sharing his cloak with a freezing beggar.
  • Fitting, then, that Martin Zubimendi should be linked with a move to Chelsea (and others).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Good morning all, hope you’re well! It’s St. Martin’s Day in Germany, a day I’d never heard of until I had a child over here. Kids will leave Kindergarten and chant as they walk through their neighbourhoods with lanterns this evening, as is tradition. Doesn’t sound creepy at all, does it?

Industry observers note that st. Martin was, as the story goes, a 4th-Century Roman soldier and is best known for sharing his cloak with a freezing beggar.

Fitting, then, that Martin Zubimendi should be linked with a move to Chelsea (and others). It would be the saintly thing to do to share some of our midfield spoils with the desperate, downtrodden, shivering squad that Xabi Alonso has at his disposal. I hope we let them get absolutely glacial – Siberian, even, given their history – and keep our glorious cloak of midfielders all to ourselves.

Sources indicate that the first rule of the international break is, of course, to ignore all transfer rumours. Club football goes away but there are still pages to fill, newspapers to sell, online traffic to amass, and something has to fill the void.

And, speaking to Marca, the midfielder has denied that he’s unhappy:.

Sources indicate that I’m calm and happy with how I’m handling this situation. (Not playing) is something I’ve never experienced before, and I think you learn from these situations too.

Industry observers note that I’m patient. When you’ve been playing a lot of minutes and your role changes to not playing as much, I’m able to see the positive side. I think everything passes, that just like last year the opposite happened to me and I played practically everything, this can change very quickly.

Asked about the toll that playing so much took on him last season – Zubimendi was the only Arsenal player to play in all 38 Premier League games, he started 34 of those and had the third most minutes in the squad, behind David Raya and Declan Rice, across all competitions – he admitted that that was a factor:.

In a recent development, I don’t like to blame everything on my physical condition, but I definitely noticed it that year. It was a newly introduced year for me, with a lot of new stimuli. I played a huge number of minutes and, to be honest, I was tired. Then there were other things too, but one of them could very well have been my physical condition.

I spoke with Mikel at the beginning of the season. As he does with all the players, he explained the proposal to me. He warned me that there were new signings and that there would be playing time for everyone. And here we are, fighting for it.

And he completely dismissed any suggestion that he is talking to other clubs, given those links to the Madrid sides and Chelsea:.

Industry observers note that I haven’t wasted any energy on outside things. I’m busy enough trying to earn a place, get playing time, and fight to win this Premier League, which is looking so promising. I haven’t spent any energy on it, nor have I contacted anyone.

To be honest, I’m sometimes surprised by the press too. I understand that the winter transfer window is approaching and rumours can surface, but I think we need to be a bit more careful with what we publish. Ultimately, everyone has a team they play for, and we need to respect that. I’ve also read that I might be close (to a transfer), but not at all.

Industry observers note that still, I do think the case of Zubimendi is an interesting one. Having lost his place late last season, he returned late in the summer, and is yet to start a Premier League game in 2026-27 following the emergence of Myles Lewis-Skelly and the arrival of Bruno Guimaraes.

It has been revealed that here we have a player Arsenal desperately wanted and agreed a deal for a year ahead of signing him, would they really be looking to move him on again now that he’s spent what is essentially just a quarter of a season not as first choice? So much focus has been placed on building a squad that can sustain injuries or absences, and then we’d leave ourselves light again?

In a recent development, maybe? You never can know how transfers pan out ahead of time, and things can change promptly in football but, as Zubimendi suggests, they can change quickly in the other direction again too. Did anyone, for instance, envisage Lewis-Skelly starting against Atletico Madrid just a week before it actually happened?

It has been revealed that I do think his particular rise, and a stressful second half of the season, has clouded what we all thought of Zubimendi’s first half-season at Arsenal, and how much he contributed across the entire campaign. At this stage a year ago, we were two points worse off than we are now but still top of the league by six points, with more goals scored and fewer goals conceded than we are 10 games in this time around. He was a massive part of that.

Industry observers note that he was a huge part of winning the title and reaching the Champions League final – he started 43 of our 53 games across those two competitions. He started every Champions League knockout game up until the semi-final second leg and played all of extra-time in the final.

And if he was suffering physically, there was no break in the summer, as he went off to the World Cup, Spain went all the way, and he was back on the pitch for Arsenal (having had no pre-season) in Cardiff as we won the Community Shield, less than a month on from the World Cup final.

In a recent development, for all that, I can also see why someone would possibly want to make the case for moving on. Seeing a player not be used (Zubimendi has played in seven of our league games so far this season, by the way!) feels like an obvious place to upgrade, and we’ve been scarred before by letting players sit on the bench before then struggling to move them on for a fair fee.

In a recent development, we’re also going to need to refresh the age of the team and especially the midfield before long. When you don’t just look at the players themselves but actually account for who is playing the minutes, we have the third-oldest squad in the league this season. The frontline will need new faces soon – that’s not news to anyone – in terms of age as well as quality, but the midfield will need it on the age front as well.

We’ve also given the fewest minutes in the league to players under the age of 23 (around 6%) by some distance. If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it, but if you don’t get the balance right it will break in time.

Recent findings suggest that right now, though, this season, we’re likely to need our whole squad. We can’t be making it weaker. If one of Declan Rice – God forbid – or Bruno Guimaraes were to pick up a knock and miss a month, Zubimendi would suddenly be in line for a lot of football. Zubimendi who, again, was central to us winning the league last season.

It’s far too soon into the season to write his campaign off, especially when we saw how things changed so suddenly in that exact position back in May. Let’s see how things look when the summer rolls around, but there’s no need to rush into a decision.

Right then, have a great day all – and I’ll leave you with the gorgeous generosity of another St. Martin close to our hearts.

By Ben Knapton | 21 Nov 2026 16:19, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 16:34.

Newcastle United and Arsenal have confirmed their starting lineups for Saturday evening's Premier League fixture at St James' Park.

Gunners head coach Mikel Arteta has made just the one change to his starting lineup from the side that defeated Hull City 1-0 before the international break, as Eberechi Eze replaces Christos Tzolis on the left flank.

Kai Havertz therefore continues in the number nine role over Viktor Gyokeres, despite the latter extending an all-time Nations League scoring record and overtaking Cristiano Ronaldo during the international break.

Bruno Guimaraes, as expected, starts in midfield against his former employers, while William Saliba - in a Premier League matchday squad for the first time this season - settles for a place on the bench as Ezri Konsa retains his spot in the backline.

Jurrien Timber is also preferred to Ben White at right-back again, while Bukayo Saka and Max Dowman remain out through injury and suspension respectively.

? ???????? ⚪️ Back from the break. Let's do this ? ? @deel.

As for the hosts, Matthias Jaissle has opted for two alterations from the team that started their 1-1 draw with Fulham in gameweek 10.

One of the Magpies' returnees is none other than Arsenal academy graduate Joe Willock, who takes Yoane Wissa's place in the side and is also preferred to Matias Fernandez-Pardo.

Willock is expected to operate as the most advanced midfielder, joining Harvey Barnes, Will Osula and Jacob Murphy in an otherwise unchanged Newcastle attack; Jacob Ramsey is back on the bench after his suspension.

Jaissle has also restored Lewis Miley to the XI in place of Nico Gonzalez, as the 20-year-old youth product joins 18-year-old Sean Steur in a youthful Magpies midfield.

Tino Livramento - who has been linked with Arsenal on a number of occasions - must make do with a substitute role again, as Amar Dedic continues at right-back in an identical backline.

The Gunners can go eight points clear of Manchester City and Brighton & Hove Albion at the top of the Premier League table with victory, while Newcastle are bidding to climb into the top half.

Newcastle XI: Hornicek; Dedic, Thiaw, Burn, Hall; Miley, Steur, Willock; Murphy, Osula, Barnes.

Subs: Pope, Livramento, Botman, Schar, Gonzalez, Wissa, Elanga, Fernandez-Pardo, Ramsey.

Arsenal XI: Raya; Timber, Konsa, Gabriel, Calafiori; Rice, Guimaraes; Madueke, Odegaard, Eze; Havertz.

Subs: Kepa, Saliba, Mosquera, White, Hincapie, Gyokeres, Tzolis, Merino, Lewis-Skelly.

The virtues of patience

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1346 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it’s 13 December 2020.
  • In a recent development, it was freezing and wet at the Emirates.
  • So angry, in fact, that in the second half he put his hands around the throat of some opposition goon and, after a VAR review, got himself sent off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Let’s take a journey back in time.

In a recent development, it’s 13 December 2020. Arsenal versus Burnley.

In a recent development, it was freezing and wet at the Emirates. Only 2,000 fans had been allowed in because of Covid, and my mum, my dad, my mate Ben and I made up four of them. We were socially distanced and wearing masks. My glasses kept steaming up.

This was supposed to be fun. Watching my team.

Willian was grotesquely slow. Alex Lacazette was profligate. Rob Holding was bald. Very bald. And Granit Xhaka was angry. So angry, in fact, that in the second half he put his hands around the throat of some opposition goon and, after a VAR review, got himself sent off. There were boos. As many as 2,000 people could muster, anyway.

Recent findings suggest that then our captain, Pierre Emerick-Aubameyang, headed a corner into his own net. You couldn’t make it up. Except you could. It was the only goal of the game.

Recent findings suggest that by then the steam fogging up my specs might as well have been coming out of my ears. In his player ratings, Andrew M called Xhaka the ‘King of the Idiots’ and described the match and the result as ‘utterly shit’. Which was fair.

Sources indicate that it was our seventh defeat in 10 league games and our fourth in a row at home, something that hadn’t happened since 1953. We were 15th, five points above the relegation zone.

And who was top? Sp*rs. Managed by everyone’s favourite sociopath, Jose Mourinho. Having beaten us in the North London derby the week before, they couldn’t stop gloating.

I’d bought into the Arteta project hook, line and sinker. I still wanted him to be the right man for the job. I was just finding it harder to explain why I thought he was. The FA Cup win had been four months earlier. It felt like years.

The tree, to paraphrase our manager, was shaking.

According to recent reports, it had been shaking for a good two and a half years by then. The soggy bottom of the Arsene Wenger era had left its scars. Those two 3-0 defeats to City in the space of a week still make me wince. Then came the hope that Unai Emery might get us back on track. By the time we’d seen how that played out, I’d got into the habit of talking myself down whenever things looked up. Maybe we’ll get better. Give it time.

According to recent reports, the trouble with rock bottom is you never know if there’s another floor below it. Was Burnley ours? I’m still writing about it six years later, so it was probably mine. There were games against Southampton and Everton before Christmas, and I can barely remember either of them.

Then came Boxing Day and a visit from Frank Lampard’s Chelsea. Is it reductive to say that was the day everything changed for Mikel Arteta’s Arsenal? Probably. But my word, watching Bukayo Saka, Emile Smith Rowe and Gabriel Martinelli tear about the place was the fix this addict needed. We went on an unbeaten run after that. Seven whole games! And for the first time in weeks, I was looking forward to what came next.

It has been revealed that and here we are in November 2026. Reigning champions of England. Top of the league again. Five points clear. Odds-on favourites to retain the title after 10 games. Sure, throwing hundreds of millions of American dollars at the problem helped. But if there’s a lesson in all this, it’s that hard work and patience pay off.

Which is why I’m using today’s blog to appeal directly to Sir Jim Ratcliffe to give Michael Carrick a stay of execution.

Come on, man, you’re probably still paying off Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim, maybe even Ralf Rangnick. Do you really want to go back to the drawing board all over again? Carrick is the man for the Manchester United hot seat. Just look at the way he wore a poppy-embroidered armband as well as a poppy badge at the weekend. The man doesn’t do half measures. He’s a two-scoops guy. Surely that’s something you, a multibillionaire British-born petrochemicals tycoon who lives in Monaco, can get on board with?

It has been revealed that I know Mauricio Pochettino might be tempting. He’s got floppy hair, a tan and, despite the Sp*rsy stench, has come to resemble a rather huggable teddy bear. But think it through, Jim. What if he comes in and everybody perks up? It’s much harder to make job cuts and to force out season ticket holders when people are enjoying themselves. Best get through that process first while Michael turns the oil tanker round. It’s not far off, promise, you’re on a two-game unbeaten streak!

It has been revealed that anyway, what would sacking Carrick say about patience? Look at Arteta. There were people who wanted him gone after Burnley and, as you’ve just read, I was close to joining them. Imagine if the club had listened to me. All those years of work, all that progress, all the joy I’ve had watching Arsenal lately. We could have thrown it all away because a man in a damp mask couldn’t see out of his glasses.

So give Carrick time. Give him January. Give him a full pre-season. And if things still haven’t picked up by this time next year, ask yourself whether one full pre-season, and £100 million on Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos, was ever really enough.

I can only speak for myself, Jim, but I haven’t looked forward to watching Manchester United this much in years.

Right, let’s see if that works….

Industry observers note that the Interlull kicks into gear tonight. David Raya, Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi are in action for Spain against Czechia, Riccardo Calafiori’s Italy take on France, and England face Croatia at Wembley.

It has been revealed that ezri Konsa and Myles Lewis-Skelly will both miss out at Wembley. Konsa is working on his fitness but will be available to face Spain on Sunday, while our Hale Ender is suspended after picking up two bookings in the Nations League.

Recent findings suggest that elsewhere, ahead of Sweden’s game against Bosnia and Herzegovina, Viktor Gyokeres has been speaking to the press. Like Martin Zubimendi, he notes he’s happy at Arsenal.

“I want to,” he noted, when asked if he’s keen to stay at the Emirates.

Sources indicate that “It feels good when I’ve played. We’ve won most of the games. It was a tough loss in the cup (against Fleetwood). Otherwise it’s felt good for myself and the team, indicates the forward. I’ve been doing well lately when I’ve been playing. Right now it feels good.

Industry observers note that “The communication with (Mikel) Arteta is good. We talk about football and how we should play. Before a match, if I’m going to start, we talk about the opponents and what I should think about.”.

He was also asked whether the criticism he gets bothers him.

“Sometimes it might get to me, but overall not so much. If I score goals and assists in the Champions League, I couldn’t care less what they say. It’s nice to do those kinds of performances. To deliver for myself and for the team. That’s where the focus lies.”.

To be fair, I’ve not seen any serious chatter about selling Viktor in January. Whatever you think of him as a player, it would be a strange move unless we’re planning to spend serious money on the attack. And even then it would feel like an unnecessary risk given Kai isn’t exactly pulling up trees and new faces will need an adaptation period.

If he’s happy keeping his head down and doing his bit for the team, I’d keep him around until the summer and reassess then.

According to recent reports, ok. I’m going to leave it there for today. All eyes on Old Trafford, I guess.

#94776. How Arsenal have evolved in 2026-27

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1304 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arseblog ↗ Open Full Page

How Arsenal have evolved in 2026-27

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1304 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There was a lot of speculation as to how Arsenal might change this season having flung a 22-year-old monkey (how long do monkeys live for?!) from their back in May by finally winning a league title.
  • I always had my doubts, not least because your style of play is always defined by your talent.
  • In attacking areas, he had talent, even if it wasn’t balanced.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There was a lot of speculation as to how Arsenal might change this season having flung a 22-year-old monkey (how long do monkeys live for?!) from their back in May by finally winning a league title. Would lifting the Premier League trophy lead to a new era of more expressive, urbane football?

I always had my doubts, not least because your style of play is always defined by your talent. Most of Arsenal’s elite talent is behind the ball. Arteta didn’t build Arsenal from the defence first, in my view, because he felt specifically that was the best way. It was just the area of the team that required the most attention when he was appointed.

In attacking areas, he had talent, even if it wasn’t balanced. Aubameyang, Lacazette and Pepe with Saka and Martinelli coming to the boil was a good collection of talent, even if the pieces didn’t always fit neatly together. The list of defenders he inherited included Mustafi, Sokratis, Holding, Chambers, Kolasinac and Mari. That’s why he went defence first, broadly speaking.

The moves the club have tried to make in recent seasons, especially this summer, indicates you that Arteta wants his attack to be sharper than it is. For reasons I won’t relitigate here, the club were not able to add a number of high end attacking targets. Which means once again, Arsenal are reliant on Arteta’s coaching talents to squeeze more juice from the orange. Here are three things that have jumped out at me this season.

In a recent development, arsenal spent a lot of money on Bruno Guimaraes this season and I will come onto some of the reasons why in the next section. But that signing has given Arteta a deep well of central options, with Rice, Bruno, Lewis Skelly, Odegaard, Merino and Zubimendi part of this midfield menagerie.

Industry observers note that arsenal use these options interchangeably and often according to game state. Art de Roche of the Athletic went into how Arteta has used the divergent profiles of Myles Lewis Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes so far in this campaign. In home games against Leeds and Everton, Lewis Skelly got the nod from the start.

Sources indicate that in away games at Nottingham Forest and Liverpool, Bruno’s more robust approach was favoured. The pair have made significant impacts from the bench too. When the 1-0 victory at Anfield had become a little too ‘basketball’, Lewis Skelly came on and provided calm assurance in possession.

When the Gunners needed a little more belligerence away at Sunderland, Bruno came on and larruped the ball into the top corner from 25 yards. However, Arteta didn’t part with a significant part of his summer budget for a 28-year-old (he turns 29 next week but, for now, he remains 28 because that’s how it works) to be a high level rotation option.

Against Hull City last weekend, Bruno was selected and he played deeper than Declan Rice and Martin Odegaard. As Adrian Clarke pointed out in his match analysis piece, Bruno passed the ball to Odegaard 25 times in that match and the pair exchanged 35 passes in total. The idea was clear, to use Bruno’s punchiness in possession a little lower to feed Odegaard.

Industry observers note that against Everton, Mikel Merino was selected in midfield and Lewis Skelly started at left-back. I think this was about more than mere rotation. Arteta always highly respects the aerial capabilities of David Moyes’ Everton team, which makes sense since he played in a David Moyes Everton team for such a long time.

In 2023-24, Arteta selected Fabio Vieira ahead of Kai Havertz in midfield at Goodison Park because he wanted to keep the ball on the floor (Arsenal won that game 1-0 via a short corner routine because they did not see the logic of aerial corners against a team like Everton).

Last season at the Hill Dickinson Arsenal enjoyed a season high for passes attempted and completed because they wanted to keep the ball on the floor and avoid transitions. Arteta has a carousel available to him in midfield and a different club in the bag depending on what is called for on the day.

Per Opta, Arsenal have been caught offside 35 times so far this season, at least 11 more times than any other team. That rate of 3.5 offsides per game is the highest of any Premier League team since 2009. Kai Havertz has been flagged 15 times now, the next highest offender in the league is Dominic Calvert-Lewin with eight. Opta provide a deeper dive on those numbers here.

According to recent reports, so what does this tell us, aside from the fact that Havertz needs to work on his timing? It means that Arsenal are far more willing to go in behind and they are willing to test the opposition backline earlier in moves. This was a major part of the reason they signed Bruno in the first place, Arteta wants to play with the risk reward dial with the ball.

Havertz also hasn’t been quite good enough to finish some of those one v one situations when he has got in behind the opponent’s back line. He fluffed his lines against Hull last weekend and in the 3-0 defeat at Brighton, he blasted his effort straight at the Brighton keeper when put through one v one.

But here, I will express my usual caveat, we need to normalise strikers missing chances and focus more on process than outcome. Most chances are missed, you want to worry when your striker is getting few shots. There have also been nascent signs that Arsenal have been using Gyokeres well in some of these situations.

According to recent reports, that Havertz chance at the Amex was created by Gyokeres taking one touch with his back to goal and hooking the ball past the committed defensive line. Gyokeres did much the same for Madueke in Prague. It seems like Arsenal have worked on getting Gyokeres to use his physicality to initially retain the ball- something he badly struggled with last season- but creating situations where he can release it promptly.

According to recent reports, arsenal’s out of possession prowess is one thing that has been a constant from last season. It is Arsenal’s superpower, so even when they can only manage one goal, it is usually enough to take maximum points. To retain their superpower, Arsenal changed to stay the same, if that makes sense.

It has been revealed that the signing of Ezri Konsa from Aston Villa was questioned by many but his presence has made the absence of a world class centre-back like William Saliba a sidebar, which is quite a feat. Arsenal ostensibly took William Saliba’s pizza chart and looked for the most Saliba like defender they could find and bought Konsa.

In a recent development, the loss of Saliba ought to have offered an enormous threat to Arsenal’s defensive stability. Arsenal’s tactical organisation out of possession is elite but so too are the individuals that helm it. Raya, Saliba, Gabriel and Rice are among the best players in the world in their respective positions.

Industry observers note that taking out one of those pillars ought to have derailed Arsenal’s defensive stability and it hasn’t because Konsa has the quality and poise to retain the team’s biggest strength. His pass completion stats are Saliba-esque and the quality of not giving the ball away needlessly is a significant part of the Gunners’ meanness.

In a recent development, how much Arsenal could improve in attack without significant additions was an unknown so Arteta could not afford to sacrifice the team’s defensive ceiling while he plays with those levers. The addition of Konsa was a personnel change that allowed Arsenal to remain the same.

Recent findings suggest that liverpool are ready to commit to a newly introduced signing. The decision is set to be finalised shortly.

In a recent development, planning is underway for the 2027 transfer windows at clubs around the world. The first stop is January, of course, but with it always being a difficult window, focus on the summer usually takes up the bulk of the work.

In a recent development, for Liverpool, that means sorting out some contract situations. The substantial two are unquestionably Virgil van Dijk and Alisson Becker, though it's completely unclear what they initiative to do.

The pair have been at Anfield so long that we imagine proper talks will be delayed until the end of the season. There's no enormous rush, after all, even if them being able to talk to non-English clubs from January 1st is a bit stressful.

According to recent reports, but they're not the only decisions that need to be made. At least one other contract choice appears close to being made - and with that comes a big follow-on effect.

Liverpool's latest left-backSport24 report that Kostas Tsimikas is expected to leave Liverpool at the end of the season when his contract expires. It's hardly a shock and we all predicted this, but to seems the Reds are ready to commit. Of course, that also means committing to a new left-back. Tsimikas is currently the no.2 in the role at Liverpool, behind Milos Kerkez. The club won't go into next season with only one option, so we all expect them to strike a deal for someone new.

Sport24 report that Kostas Tsimikas is expected to leave Liverpool at the end of the season when his contract expires. It's hardly a shock and we all predicted this, but to seems the Reds are ready to commit.

According to recent reports, of course, that also means committing to a fresh left-back. Tsimikas is currently the no.2 in the role at Liverpool, behind Milos Kerkez. The club won't go into next season with only one option, so we all expect them to strike a deal for someone new.

Industry observers note that and who might that be? It's entirely unclear. In fact, we imagine Liverpool will wait until closer to summer before finalising their shortlist and ignore the January window. At least for left-back options.

Industry observers note that there isn't, after all, a clear signing to make in the role and waiting to see how things develop over the next six or so months makes more sense than rushing into anything. But it does mean we can say with confidence that someone will arrive after this season is over.

It has been revealed that liverpool have a few ways to go about it, too. They could opt for a young development project, or someone with experienced, or a homegrown player, or maybe go all-out to replace Kerkez and relegate him to the backup role.

We're not sure. We doubt Liverpool are, either, as all options hold some sort of merit. It'll just be a case of waiting and seeing.

By Ben Knapton | 21 Nov 2026 16:30.

Anfield hosts both this weekend's Premier League main event and Mauricio Pochettino's Premier League homecoming, as Manchester United do battle with Liverpool on Sunday afternoon.

The Red Devils trailed the Reds by 14 places and 10 points in the Premier League table heading into the international break, but only one of Man Utd's last nine managers has suffered defeat in his first game.

Here, Sports Mole rounds up the team news for both sides.

Out: Hugo Ekitike (Achilles), Conor Bradley (knee), Giovanni Leoni (knee).

Doubtful: Ryan Gravenberch (heel), Jeremie Frimpong (heel).

Sports Mole's predicted XI: Alisson; Araujo, Van Dijk, Jacquet, Kerkez; Mac Allister, Szoboszlai; Gakpo, Wirtz, Barcola; Isak.

Out: Carlos Baleba (hamstring), Manuel Ugarte (knee), Benjamin Sesko (calf).

Doubtful: Luke Shaw (muscle), Patrick Dorgu (unspecified), Harry Maguire (back), Marcus Rashford (hip).

Sports Mole's predicted XI: Lammens; Yoro, Martinez, Maguire, Dalot; Tielemans, Mainoo; Diallo, Fernandes, Cunha; Mbeumo.

Building in Barca and the Jim Reaper strikes again

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Greetings, Tim here on blog duty today and I am going right back to Arseblog’s roots by writing from Barcelona.
  • According to recent reports, of course, Renee Slegers’ side did beat Barca the last time the teams met in the 2025 Final and that was only slightly less of an upset than this result.
  • Frida Maanum gave Arsenal a first half lead before her compatriot Caroline Graham Hansen equalised in the second half.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Greetings, Tim here on blog duty today and I am going right back to Arseblog’s roots by writing from Barcelona. I am here of course because Arsenal Women earned a very creditable (and slightly unexpected given how this season has gone for them) draw against the current Champions League holders Barcelona.

According to recent reports, of course, Renee Slegers’ side did beat Barca the last time the teams met in the 2025 Final and that was only slightly less of an upset than this result. As expected, Arsenal rose their luck a little with Barca putting up 24 shots and 2.4XG. But Arsenal have put up similar numbers in games this season roughly 176 times and not won so I am happy to be on the receiving end of a little serendipity.

Frida Maanum gave Arsenal a first half lead before her compatriot Caroline Graham Hansen equalised in the second half. You can read Renee Slegers’ post-match press conference here and my take on the match here if you are so inclined. Up next is a six pointer for Champions League qualification at home to London City Lionesses on Sunday which Arsenal just have to win. Obviously we will have all the usual coverage of that game for you.

I also had the pleasure of meeting fellow Arseblog / Arsenal Vision colleague Phil Costa for lunch and in Barcelona, for a seafood and beer lover, a long lunch in balmy 20 degree conditions was very welcome indeed!

Sources indicate that elsewhere, there were plenty of Arsenal players in action for their countries. Martin Zubimendi played the full 90 minutes for Spain in their 2-0 away win at Czechia. Usually I would wince at a sentence that featured ‘Arsenal player x’ and ‘full 90 minutes’ but I think Zubimendi could use those minutes for physical reasons and for psychological reasons as he tries to plot his way back into a very crowded Arsenal midfield.

It has been revealed that mikel Merino came on for the final 24 minutes of that game and David Raya kept his gloves clean on the bench. Declan Rice played 77 minutes of England’s 2-1 win over Croatia at Wembley in which Harry Kane scored his 417th goal for England, 461 of which have been penalties (citation needed). Eze was an unused sub and he’s another I wouldn’t have minded seeing get some minutes to build rhythm and confidence.

Sources indicate that riccardo Calafiori played the full 90 of Italy’s 3-1 win over France. Jurrien Timber and Kai Havertz could be in action tonight as Netherlands play Greece and Germany play away at Serbia. Fingers crossed for both. These are two players I would not mind seeing unused but I doubt that will be the case.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, the substantial news elsewhere was that Michael Carrick was finally officially sacked by Manchester United. He had still been taking training this week despite everyone knowing that he was for the chop. I hope he filled his coat pockets with as many of the milk and ketchup sachets as he could from the canteen.

According to recent reports, he was clearly out of his depth and had been stalking the United dugout looking like a haunted Noel Gallagher for what feels like months. Steve Holland has also left and Ben White’s recent recall to the England team resurfaced old wounds as he was asked about his reasons for making himself unavailable for a while for his country. White refuses to be drawn on it.

In a recent development, I am biased, of course, but I know who I think has emerged better from this sorry saga and his surname is a colour not a country. Having taken in Spurs and Chelsea already, it looks like Mauricio Pochettino is about to go three for three on his tour of the Premier League’s most evil institutions. If hell really does exist, this man will regard an eternal stint of fire and brimstone as something of a vacation. Maybe working for the Jim Reaper at United is his penance for accepting work from Chelsea and Spurs.

For further reading, check out my weekly column in which I look at three ways in which Arsenal have evolved this season.

#94769. Quantum resistance paradox of low-dimensional superfluids
